chief_complaint: sudden racing heartbeat, dizziness, and throat tightness for 15 minutes
hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden racing heartbeat, dizziness, and throat tightness for 15 minutes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he is having an acute allergic reaction to something he ate for lunch because his throat feels tight and his heart is pounding.
concerns: He is terrified that his racing heart is going to suddenly give out and trigger a fatal cardiac arrest.
expectations: He hopes to receive a quick injection or medication to slow his heart rate back down to normal.

investigation_events.title: 12-lead ECG during palpitations
investigation_events.availability_message: The ECG recorded during the palpitations is now available.

results.value: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 186 bpm with QRS 84 ms and no clearly visible preceding P waves

clinical_knowledge.topic: Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management begins with ECG assessment and haemodynamic stability; stable regular narrow-complex SVT may be treated with vagal manoeuvres then monitored IV adenosine, while unstable tachyarrhythmia requires synchronized cardioversion.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden racing heartbeat, dizziness, and throat tightness for 15 minutes

Key HPI features: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden racing heartbeat, dizziness, and throat tightness for 15 minutes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Paroxysmal SVT.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Atrial fibrillation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Episodes with chest pain, syncope, or breathlessness at rest.
management_principles: Obtain ECG and assess haemodynamic stability; for stable regular narrow-complex SVT, use vagal manoeuvres then monitored IV adenosine, while unstable tachyarrhythmia requires synchronized cardioversion
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A re-entry circuit produces sudden, regular, very fast palpitations — often with a pounding sensation in the throat.
red_flags: Episodes with chest pain, syncope, or breathlessness at rest

must_ask.say: Does it start instantly, or build up over minutes?
Do you feel a pounding in your neck or throat with it?
Is the fast beat completely regular?
Does bearing down or holding your breath ever stop it?
Have you fainted or felt like you were going to?
How often does this happen, and has it stopped you doing anything?

history.answer: My heart suddenly started racing about fifteen minutes ago, and I feel dizzy and tight in my throat.
My heart feels like it is running away at an extremely fast, constant speed. It doesn't skip beats or jump around, it just beats furiously fast.
I can tap it out like this—it is completely regular, like a very rapid machine gun tapping without any pauses.
It started abruptly out of nowhere while I was sitting down, like flipping a light switch on. It hasn't stopped yet.
I feel an intense fluttering and pounding sensation right at the base of my throat, which makes it feel tight.
This episode has lasted fifteen minutes so far. I had a couple of brief racing flutters a few months ago, but they only lasted a minute and stopped on their own.
I was just sitting at my desk working when it kicked in. I haven't exercised, changed positions quickly, or had any major emotional stress today.
I tried drinking cold water and taking deep breaths to calm down, but it didn't change anything. I haven't tried bearing down or holding my breath yet.
I feel quite lightheaded and woozy since it started, but I haven't passed out or lost consciousness.

I don't have any sharp or squeezing chest pain, just that uncomfortable fullness in my chest and throat. My breathing feels a bit shallow because of how fast it's beating, but I'm not gasping for air.
No, I haven't had trouble with the heat, increased sweating, weight loss, or hand shaking before today.
I do feel generally tired and washed out right now. But I haven't had black or bloody stools, unusual bruising, or chronic fatigue before this.
No, I don't have a severe headache or profuse sweating, and I haven't had episodes where I suddenly turn pale with a racing heart.
I felt startled and anxious when my heart suddenly took off, but I didn't have sudden overwhelming dread, tingling in my fingers, or a panic attack before it started.
No, I haven't had a cold, sore throat, cough, or any fever recently.
I had one cup of regular coffee this morning around 8 AM, which is my usual routine. I don't drink energy drinks.
I thought maybe I was having a severe food allergy reaction from lunch, since my throat feels tight and my heart suddenly took off.
I'm terrified that my heart is beating so fast it's going to suddenly give out on me.
I just want you to give me something right away to slow my heart back down to a normal pace.
I have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, or any thyroid trouble. Aside from those brief flutters, I've always been healthy.
I've never had any surgeries and I've never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter cold drugs, diet pills, or herbal supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend with friends, and I haven't had any alcohol in the past few days.
I work as an office clerk, and I live with my wife in an apartment.
No one in my family has had sudden unexplained death, early heart attacks, or known heart rhythm problems.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 114/74 mmHg, pulse is 186 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and temperature is 36.6°C.
The patient is alert, visibly anxious, mildly diaphoretic, and resting in no acute respiratory distress.
Radial and carotid pulses are extremely rapid, regular, and symmetric, with no pulse deficit.
Regular tachycardia at approximately 186 beats per minute with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops are heard.
Clear vesicular breath sounds throughout both lung fields without wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
Jugular venous pulse shows rapid undulations without frank distension; jugular venous pressure is within normal limits.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are anicteric.
No exophthalmos, lid lag, or conjunctival injection noted; pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light.
The thyroid gland is normal in size and texture, without palpable nodules, tenderness, or bruits.
No fine postural tremor is observed when arms are extended.
No peripheral edema in the lower extremities; distal extremities are warm and well perfused.
